clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-based permutation tests (5000 permutations) with FDR correction (p<0.05) to compare overlap maps between clinical groups and HC(test); Mann-Whitney U tests to compare number of extreme deviations per subject between groups; Network-based statistics (NBS) with permutation tests (n=5000) to identify significant network differences between HC and clinical groups using both raw functional connectivity and z-scores; Spearman correlation between global deviation scores (average z-scores of extreme deviations) and clinical assessment scores (total ADOS for ASD); comparisons of spectral power and functional connectivity distributions between sexes within diagnostic groups using Wilcoxon Rank-Sum tests with Cohen's d effect sizes; correlations with IQ scores (WISC FSIQ); overlap analysis limited to subjects with at least one extreme deviation; stratification by primary diagnosis despite comorbidity; sensitivity analyses on subjects with only one diagnosis.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Deviations from normative EEG patterns in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders were highly heterogeneous and frequency-dependent, with spatial overlap not exceeding 40% for spectral power and 24% for functional connectivity across patients, and individual deviations showed significant correlations with clinical assessments (ADOS scores in ASD).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study demonstrated substantial electrophysiological heterogeneity in ADHD, ASD, anxiety, and learning disorders using normative modeling of HD-EEG. Key findings include: (1) Spatial overlap of extreme deviations was low, not exceeding 40% for spectral power (e.g., delta: ADHD 31%, ANX 32%; beta: ASD 28%, HC(test) 31%; gamma: LD 40%) and 24% for functional connectivity (e.g., alpha: HC(test) 14%, ASD 9%, ADHD 10%, LD 10%; gamma: ANX 12%), calculated among subjects with at least one extreme deviation. (2) Percentages of subjects with at least one negative spectral deviation were relatively low (highest: theta ASD 44%, alpha ADHD 29%). (3) For functional connectivity, higher percentages showed at least one negative deviation (up to 87% in delta HC(test), 82% theta ADHD). (4) Group-based permutation tests revealed frequency-dependent and disorder-specific patterns; for spectral features, only 15 channels survived FDR correction for LD in beta band, 11 channels for ANX in gamma; for positive deviations, 74 channels remained significant for ADHD in gamma after FDR. (5) Network-based statistics using z-scores (but not raw FC) identified significant differences between HC and clinical groups: ASD showed differences in alpha (p=0.0002, 91 edges) and beta (p=0.007, 12 edges); ADHD in delta (p<0.0001, 94 edges). (6) Global deviation scores showed significant but modest Spearman correlations with total ADOS scores in ASD (ρ≈0.2, p<0.05), with positive deviations increasing and negative deviations decreasing as ADOS scores increased. (7) Heterogeneity was observed in both clinical and control groups, highlighting complexity beyond simple case-control distinctions. (8) Clinical cohorts showed varying numbers of extreme deviations compared to HC, without uniform trends, suggesting individual-specific rather than group-consistent patterns.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Sample size moderate for EEG but not large-scale like MRI studies; unequal dataset contributions (HBN: 1539/2234 subjects); limited to 128-channel systems affecting generalizability; cross-sectional data limiting assessment of within-subject variability and developmental trajectories; restricted age range (5-18 years) encompassing only developmental stages; comorbidity complexity with multiple diagnoses; potential medication effects on EEG signals; limited feature set (spectral power and connectivity); inability to train multivariate GAMLSS models requiring individual models per channel/connection; lack of longitudinal data to distinguish stable vs transient variations
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: While our sample size is considered significantly large for EEG studies (n ~ 2200), it does not reach the scale often seen in MRI and fMRI studies, nor is it representative of the broader population. Furthermore, the sample size of the datasets was not uniform. The largest dataset, HBN, comprised 1539 subjects out of the total 2234 subjects... data for this article has been sourced from five studies... utilizing 128-channel EEG systems. While this somewhat controls for variability... it also introduces limitations to the generalizability... our NM results are based on cross-sectional data, capturing individual deviations at a single time point. This limits our ability to assess within-subject variability and developmental trajectories... the population included in the study has a restricted age range (5-18 years), encompassing only younger, developmental stages... Another challenge of the study stems from the inherent heterogeneity that may exist within each group of patients who present multiple psychiatric diagnoses... Another limitation of this study is the potential influence of medication on EEG results... our choice of the features to model was based on the most dominant features in the literature... Presently, the capability to train normative models for multiple response variables using GAMLSS is unavailable, thereby limiting modeling versatility.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Downsampling strategy for larger diagnostic groups (ADHD, ANX) while ensuring balanced representation across age, sex, and site/study covariates; consideration of comorbidity with primary diagnosis approach and sensitivity analysis on single-diagnosis subjects; exploratory sex-difference analyses using Wilcoxon Rank-Sum tests with Cohen's d effect sizes; IQ correlation analyses using WISC FSIQ scores; bootstrap analysis for model stability assessment (1000 resamples); visualization of only highest 3% overlap values for connectivity maps; separate analysis of positive and negative deviations; calculation of both channel-wise/connection-wise metrics and global deviation scores; proof-of-concept demonstration that deviation scores (z-scores) can outperform raw features in group differentiation using NBS; framework positioned as foundation for developing patient-specific electrophysiological biomarkers for precision psychiatry

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a pioneering study applying normative modeling to high-density EEG in psychiatry, extending beyond the more common MRI-based normative modeling literature. The study uses five distinct datasets aggregated together, with the largest (HBN) contributing 1539/2234 subjects. Multiple diagnoses per subject were common (comorbidity detailed in Table S1), but primary diagnosis was used for group assignment. Medication use was permitted in HBN dataset (stable regimen required in ABCCT). Different preprocessing approaches were used for different datasets (e.g., Autoreject excluded for ABCCT, femaleASD already preprocessed). The study analyzed both scalp-level (124 channels) and source-level (68 ROIs from Desikan-Killiany atlas) features. Models trained separately for each channel/connection and frequency band due to GAMLSS limitations for multivariate responses. Distribution families varied by frequency band and feature type (spectral vs connectivity), selected empirically using BIC (details in Tables S4-S6). Age-specific head models were used for source reconstruction (4-18 year template). The study emphasizes moving beyond average group differences to individual-level heterogeneity characterization, positioning this as critical for precision psychiatry. Code available at https://github.com/MINDIG-1/NM-Psy.git. Authors A.E., S.A., and M.H. are full-time employees of MINDIG company. Study received funding from MINDIG R&D, French government ANR grant (EEG-MIND ANR-22-EXPR0009), Region Bretagne (Inno R&D project no. 23001155), and Rennes Metropole (AICE project).
